Campus Clubs

This worksheet assumes students already know basic retrieval. Use it to move into ORDER BY, DISTINCT, LIKE, BETWEEN, joins, and a first grouped report while reinforcing one-to-one, many-to-many, and composite-key structures.

ORDER BY DISTINCT LIKE BETWEEN JOIN GROUP BY
Open SQL Playground All SQL worksheets

Dataset

  • LOGIN_ACCOUNT is one-to-one with STUDENT
  • MEMBERSHIP is a junction table with a composite key
  • Ideal for learning join routes through an ERD

Syllabus Links

  • A3.2.2 ERDs and relationship structure
  • A3.2.4 primary keys, foreign keys, and composite keys
  • A3.3.2 ordering, pattern matching, filtering, and joins

Before You Start

  • Use the ERD to trace the join path before writing the SQL.
  • This worksheet assumes SELECT, FROM, and WHERE are already secure.
  • The grouped report at the end is a bridge into later reporting work.
1

Read the Relationships

Use the schema and ERD to describe how the tables fit together.

  1. A3.2.2 Many-to-many

    Identify the junction table and explain which many-to-many relationship it resolves.

  2. A3.2.4 Composite key

    State the composite primary key in MEMBERSHIP and explain why both fields are needed together.

  3. A3.2.2 One-to-one

    Explain why LOGIN_ACCOUNT to STUDENT is one-to-one in this model.

2

Sort, Match, and Narrow

Use next-step query clauses on one table at a time.

Reference pattern — ORDER BY, DISTINCT, LIKE, BETWEEN 
-- Sort rows
SELECT column_a, column_b
FROM table_name
ORDER BY column_a ASC, column_b ASC;

-- Return unique values only
SELECT DISTINCT category_column
FROM table_name
ORDER BY category_column;

-- Match part of a text value
SELECT *
FROM table_name
WHERE text_column LIKE '%Lab%';

-- Filter within an inclusive range
SELECT *
FROM table_name
WHERE date_column BETWEEN '2025-09-20' AND '2025-09-30';

ORDER BY controls presentation of the final result. DISTINCT removes repeated rows from the selected columns. LIKE uses % as a wildcard.

  1. A3.3.2 ORDER BY

    List every club with its meeting day and room, ordered first by MeetingDay and then by ClubName.

  2. A3.3.2 DISTINCT

    Return each unique role used in MEMBERSHIP, sorted alphabetically.

  3. A3.3.2 LIKE

    Find clubs where the meeting room contains the word Lab.

  4. A3.3.2 BETWEEN

    Show membership rows where JoinedOn falls between 2025-09-20 and 2025-09-30 inclusive.

3

Join Through the ERD

Move from entity table to entity table by following the foreign keys.

Reference pattern — JOIN through a junction table 
-- Two-table join
SELECT a.column_a, b.column_b
FROM first_table AS a
INNER JOIN second_table AS b
    ON a.primary_key = b.foreign_key;

-- Join through a junction table
SELECT s.name_column, j.role_column, c.title_column
FROM student_table AS s
INNER JOIN junction_table AS j
    ON s.student_id = j.student_id
INNER JOIN club_table AS c
    ON j.club_id = c.club_id;

-- Filter after the joins
SELECT s.name_column, c.title_column
FROM student_table AS s
INNER JOIN junction_table AS j
    ON s.student_id = j.student_id
INNER JOIN club_table AS c
    ON j.club_id = c.club_id
WHERE s.year_group = 12;

When a result needs columns from several tables, follow the relationship path one link at a time. Table aliases keep longer join queries readable.

  1. A3.3.2 JOIN 2 tables

    Join STUDENT to LOGIN_ACCOUNT and show each student’s full name, username, and last-login date.

  2. A3.3.2 JOIN 3 tables

    Show every member of Coding Collective with their role and year group. Sort by role and then surname.

  3. A3.3.2 Filtered join

    Return the full names of Year 12 students and the clubs they attend.

4

First Grouped Report

Use one grouped summary to bridge into later reporting work.

Reference pattern — COUNT and GROUP BY 
-- Count rows in each group
SELECT category_column, COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM table_name
GROUP BY category_column;

-- Group after a join
SELECT c.title_column, COUNT(*) AS member_count
FROM junction_table AS j
INNER JOIN club_table AS c
    ON j.club_id = c.club_id
GROUP BY c.title_column
ORDER BY member_count DESC;

GROUP BY creates one summary row per group. COUNT(*) tells you how many rows ended up in each group.

  1. A3.3.2 GROUP BY

    Count how many students belong to each club. Show club name and member count only.

  2. A3.3.2 COUNT

    Count how many students there are in each year group, ordered from highest year group to lowest.

Model Answers — Campus Clubs

Section 1

1
Relationships MEMBERSHIP resolves the many-to-many relationship between STUDENT and CLUB. The composite key is (StudentID, ClubID). LOGIN_ACCOUNT is one-to-one because its primary key is also the student foreign key.

Section 2

2
Sorting and matching 
SELECT ClubName, MeetingDay, MeetingRoom
FROM CLUB
ORDER BY MeetingDay, ClubName;

SELECT DISTINCT Role
FROM MEMBERSHIP
ORDER BY Role;

SELECT *
FROM CLUB
WHERE MeetingRoom LIKE '%Lab%';

Section 3

3
Join pattern 
SELECT s.FirstName, s.LastName, l.Username, l.LastLogin
FROM STUDENT AS s
INNER JOIN LOGIN_ACCOUNT AS l
    ON s.StudentID = l.StudentID;

SELECT s.FirstName, s.LastName, m.Role, s.YearGroup
FROM STUDENT AS s
INNER JOIN MEMBERSHIP AS m
    ON s.StudentID = m.StudentID
INNER JOIN CLUB AS c
    ON m.ClubID = c.ClubID
WHERE c.ClubName = 'Coding Collective'
ORDER BY m.Role, s.LastName;

Section 4

4
Grouped report 
SELECT c.ClubName, COUNT(*) AS MemberCount
FROM MEMBERSHIP AS m
INNER JOIN CLUB AS c
    ON m.ClubID = c.ClubID
GROUP BY c.ClubName
ORDER BY MemberCount DESC, c.ClubName;
